scenes.heading: Angles and parallel lines
scenes.sub: One clue leads to the next
scenes.say: You already know the F, Z and C rules. This year, the answer is a few steps away, so let's chain the rules together.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A detective follows one clue to the next
scenes.science: Each angle you find unlocks the next one, using one rule
scenes.breaks: a detective can guess. In maths every link must be a real rule you can name.
scenes.say: Think of a detective. Clue one leads to clue two, then clue three. Angle problems work the same way: each angle you find unlocks the next. But unlike a detective, you can never guess. Every link must be a rule you can name.

scenes.heading: Mark it, link it, write it
points: Link one new angle using one rule
Write the reason, e.g. (alternate, AB ∥ CD)
Repeat until you reach the target
scenes.say: Here's a made-up trick: mark it, link it, write it. Mark every angle you know. Link one new angle using one rule. Write the reason. Repeat until you reach the angle you want.

scenes.heading: Alternate angles make a Z
scenes.say: First the parallel lines, then the transversal. Angle A P Q is one hundred and twenty-eight degrees. Angle P Q D makes a Z shape with it, so it is also one hundred and twenty-eight. Angle P Q C is on a straight line with it: fifty-two.
scenes.caption: Angle APQ = 128°. Angle PQD makes a Z shape with it, so it is also 128°. Angle PQC is on a straight line with it, so it is 52°.

scenes.heading: Angles with algebra
scenes.question: Alternate angles are (3x + 14)° and (5x − 30)°. Find x and the angle.
scenes.say: Alternate angles are three x plus fourteen, and five x minus thirty. Alternate angles are equal, so set them equal. Take three x from both sides and add thirty: forty-four equals two x, so x is twenty-two. Now substitute back: three times twenty-two plus fourteen is eighty degrees.
scenes.caption: Alternate angles are equal: 3x + 14 = 5x − 30. So 44 = 2x and x = 22. Substitute back: 3 × 22 + 14 = 80°.

scenes.heading: Arrowhead: draw a third parallel line
notes: Dashed line EF is parallel to AB and CD
Top part of the tip = p
Bottom part of the tip = q
scenes.say: Here is the arrowhead. First the parallel lines, then the two arms meeting at E. Now the dashed line through E, parallel to both. The top part of the tip matches angle p at B, and the bottom part matches angle q at D. Both are alternate angles.

scenes.heading: The arrowhead rule
parts: the angle at the tip, E
top arm with the top line
bottom arm with the bottom line
scenes.say: So the tip angle always equals the two arm angles added together. Arrowhead means add!

scenes.heading: Arrowhead example
scenes.question: AB ∥ CD. ∠ABE = 35° and ∠CDE = 50°. Find the tip angle ∠BED.
lines: Draw EF parallel to AB through E
scenes.say: The arms make thirty-five and fifty degrees with the parallel lines. Draw a line through E, parallel to both. The top part of the tip is thirty-five, the bottom part is fifty, both alternate angles. So the tip angle is eighty-five degrees.
scenes.caption: Draw a parallel line through E. The top part is 35° and the bottom part is 50° (alternate angles). So the tip angle is 85°.

scenes.heading: Equal or 180?
scenes.say: Before writing an equation, decide which rule links the angles. F and Z angles: set them equal. C angles: add them to make one hundred and eighty. Then check: does the question want x, or the angle?

points: Chain rules, one reason per step
F and Z: equal. C: add to 180°
Substitute back to find the angle
Arrowhead: tip = sum of arm angles
scenes.say: Quick recap. Chain the rules one step at a time, with a reason for each. F and Z angles are equal, C angles add to one hundred and eighty. For an arrowhead, add the two arm angles. Now try the practice questions!
